identity.title: Dynamic auscultation: systolic murmur louder with Valsalva/standing, softer with squatting or handgrip

technique.how: Auscultate the murmur at the left sternal border at baseline, then during a sustained Valsalva strain (10-15 s), on rapid squat-to-stand, on standing-to-squat, and during sustained handgrip. Record whether intensity increases or decreases with each maneuver compared with baseline.
technique.prerequisites: Patient able to strain, squat and stand safely; steady baseline auscultation first; allow the murmur to re-equilibrate between maneuvers.
technique.contraindications: Valsalva/standing unsafe in presyncopal, hemodynamically unstable or frail/fall-prone patients; squatting limited by orthopaedic disease.

interpretation.positive_finding: A murmur that gets louder with Valsalva or standing and softer with squatting or handgrip indicates dynamic LVOT obstruction (HCM); Valsalva augmentation has 96% specificity.
interpretation.negative_finding: A murmur that fails to increase with squat-to-stand (95% sensitivity) argues against HCM; fixed AS murmurs typically soften with Valsalva and do not intensify on standing.
interpretation.pitfalls: Only 50 patients, cardiologist examiners, and no single maneuver is perfect; Valsalva is specific but only 65% sensitive. Mitral valve prolapse murmurs also lengthen/intensify on standing.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: HCM moves to the top of the list (echo, avoid dehydration/vasodilators, arrhythmia review). Negative: fixed obstruction (AS) or other murmur cause more likely.

estimates.population: 50 patients with documented systolic murmurs of varied cause (HCM vs all other murmurs); cardiology examiners
estimates.reference_standard: Documented cause of murmur (echocardiography/catheterization per study; abstract states 'documented systolic murmurs')
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.65/(1-0.96); LR- = (1-0.65)/0.96; sens/spec as reported in abstract (no CIs)
estimates.quote: an increase in intensity with the Valsalva maneuver (65 percent sensitivity, 96 percent specificity)

sources.citation: Lembo NJ, Dell'Italia LJ, Crawford MH, O'Rourke RA. Bedside diagnosis of systolic murmurs. N Engl J Med. 1988;318(24):1572-1578.
Etchells E, Bell C, Robb K. Does this patient have an abnormal systolic murmur? JAMA. 1997;277(7):564-571.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not perform Valsalva or rapid postural maneuvers in patients who are hypotensive, presyncopal, or at high fall risk; do not use dynamic auscultation to exclude structural disease when an echo is indicated anyway.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Exertional syncope with a dynamic murmur suggests obstructive HCM: urgent echocardiography and arrhythmia assessment; avoid volume depletion and vasodilators.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No reliability data for maneuver responses found; general systolic murmur detection has only fair agreement (kappa 0.30-0.48, Etchells 1997).

extraction_notes: All numbers from the Lembo 1988 NEJM abstract; LRs computed from reported sensitivity/specificity (no CIs available, full text not accessible). HCM comparisons are versus all other systolic murmurs, so specificity reflects a murmur-referral population rather than unselected patients. Etchells 1997 RCE summarises HCM maneuvers from smaller lower-quality studies but its tables were not viewable.
